title: Fixing bad RAG answers: a debugging playbook
hook: Find whether the fault is the source, the search, the chunks, the prompt or the model, before changing anything.
inPlainWords: When a RAG answer is wrong, there are four places it can have gone wrong: the right passage was never in the library, search did not find it, the model ignored it, or the passage itself was wrong. Checking in that order saves weeks of guessing.

useCase.title: The bot says "30 days" and the real answer is 14
useCase.story: A customer complaint arrives with a screenshot: the bot said opened electronics have a 30-day return window. The current policy says 14 days and is in the library. The team is tempted to switch models. Where should they start?

approaches.name: Change the model
approaches.what: Try a bigger or different model.
approaches.greatWhen: Only after the earlier checks pass.

approaches.name: Check the source
approaches.what: Is the right, current document in the library at all?
approaches.example: The old 30-day policy PDF is still indexed.

approaches.name: Check retrieval
approaches.what: Did search return the right passage near the top?

approaches.name: Check chunking
approaches.greatWhen: The document is there but the right text is not found.
approaches.example: The rule was split from its table.

approaches.name: Check the prompt and context
approaches.what: Did the model see the passage, and was it told to use only that?
approaches.example: The prompt lets the model use its own knowledge.

approaches.name: Check the answer against the passage
approaches.what: Did the model follow the passage faithfully?
approaches.example: The passage says 14 days, the answer says 30.

approaches.name: Add a regression test
approaches.what: Save this failure as a test case.
approaches.example: Add the question to the golden set.

challenge.question: The bot quotes 30 days but the real answer is 14. Where do you start?

options.text: Check whether the current policy is indexed and whether retrieval returned it, then the prompt, then the model, and add a regression test
options.why: It follows the pipeline in order, so each check rules out a cause.
You would be guessing, and it may not touch the real cause.
The policy was right. The pipeline was wrong.
It may help a little, but it does not find the cause.

bestCase.title: Debug in pipeline order, then lock the fix in
bestCase.example: The team finds both the old 30-day PDF and the new 14-day PDF in the index, and the old one ranks first. They remove it, add date metadata so newer documents win, re-test, and add the question to the golden set so it can never silently return.

worstCase.title: Guessing at the fix
worstCase.example: The team swaps to a bigger model, then rewrites the prompt, then changes chunk sizes. Each change moves other answers, nobody knows what fixed what, and the old PDF stays in the library.

steps.label: Reproduce the failure
steps.goes: Ask the question and save the retrieved passages.

steps.label: Is the current policy indexed?
steps.goes: Both the old 30-day PDF and the new 14-day PDF are present.
steps.goesWrong: The team swaps the model straight away, without checking.

steps.label: Did search find the passage?
steps.goes: The old PDF ranks first. That is the cause.

steps.label: Fix the source or the ranking
steps.goes: Remove the old PDF and add date metadata.

steps.label: Re-test
steps.goes: The bot now answers 14 days, with a citation.

steps.label: Add to the golden set
steps.goes: The failure becomes a permanent test.

takeaway: Debug RAG in pipeline order: source, search, chunks, prompt, model. Then turn the failure into a permanent test.
